questions.q: What does it mean that a hash function is 'one-way'?
options: There is no way to reverse a hash output back into the original input data
It can only process text input, never binary data
The same input produces a different hash every time it's computed
It only works in one direction across a network connection
questions.explain: Hashing is deliberately irreversible — you cannot mathematically recover the original input from its hash.

questions.q: Why does a well-built login system store a password's hash instead of the password itself?
options: It is required for passwords to work with SMS-based MFA
Hashes take up less disk space than the original password
Hashing makes passwords load faster during login
So the real password is never stored anywhere, and a breach of the hash database doesn't hand out working passwords directly
questions.explain: Storing only the hash means the actual password never exists in the database, so even a breach doesn't directly expose it (though weak passwords can still be cracked).

questions.q: How is a digital signature actually constructed?
options: The entire message is encrypted with the recipient's public key
It is a password shared in advance between sender and recipient
The message is hashed, then that hash is encrypted with the sender's private key
A digital signature is simply the sender's typed name appended to the message
questions.explain: A digital signature combines hashing with asymmetric encryption — hash the message, then encrypt that hash with the sender's private key.

questions.q: What two things does a valid digital signature prove about a message?
options: That it came from the claimed sender, and that it hasn't been altered since signing
That the message was sent over HTTPS
That the recipient has a valid password
Only that the message is encrypted, nothing about its sender
questions.explain: A matching signature proves authenticity (only the private-key holder could produce it) and integrity (any change would alter the hash).

questions.q: What role does a certificate authority (CA) play in PKI?
options: It has no real function in how HTTPS establishes trust
It issues digital certificates that bind a public key to a verified identity, signed with the CA's own private key
It stores the private keys of every website on the internet
It generates every user's password on their behalf
questions.explain: CAs issue and sign certificates binding a public key to an identity, and browsers verify that signature back to a trusted root CA.
